kurals.tamil:
ஒழுக்கத்து நீத்தார் பெருமை விழுப்பத்து
வேண்டும் பனுவல் துணிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ozhukkaththu neeththaar perumai vizhuppaththu,
Vendum panuval thunivu.
kurals.meaning: The settled conclusion of every worthwhile book is that the greatness of those who, standing firm in their own discipline, have let go of desire should be praised above all other excellence.
kurals.elementary: Imagine every good book in the world lined up on one shelf, and you ask them all the same question: “Who is the greatest kind of person?” This kural says they would all give the same answer — the person who keeps to good habits and stops grabbing for things they want.
kurals.university: Valluvar grounds the authority of asceticism not in revelation but in textual consensus: “panuval thunivu” means literally “the settled resolution (thunivu) of learned works (panuval).” His renunciant is “neeththaar,” “those who have let go” — a participle from nee- (to leave, to separate) rather than a sectarian title such as sannyāsin or bhikkhu, so the ascetic is defined by an act rather than by membership in an order. Crucially he binds renunciation to “ozhukkam,” disciplined conduct, refusing to let letting-go collapse into licence: greatness belongs only to those who stand “ozhukkaththu,” inside conduct. The word “vizhuppam” (pre-eminence, the choicest thing) makes the claim comparative rather than merely approving — not that renunciation is good, but that it is the highest good the books know. This opening move is characteristic of Tamil didactic poetry, which establishes authority by appeal to accumulated learned opinion, and it lets the chapter exalt renunciants without endorsing any one religion's account of why they matter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A yogī is greater than the ascetic, greater than the empiricist and greater than the fruitive worker. Therefore, O Arjuna, in all circumstances, be a yogī.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna closes the chapter on meditation by ranking the person of disciplined inner practice above the body-mortifying ascetic, above the scholar, and above the ritual performer.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's move: a canonical text explicitly ranking the disciplined renunciant at the top of every other class of person.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.46 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Both are authoritative texts issuing a comparative ranking that puts disciplined renunciation first; the small gap is that Krishna ranks the yogī above the tapasvin, while Valluvar praises the renunciant as such.

christianity.quote_or_event: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.”
christianity.explanation: The author of Hebrews ends a long roll-call of the faithful by saying that the world did not deserve those who gave up home and comfort to wander destitute in the wilderness.
christianity.tie_back: Scripture here does precisely what the Kural says scripture does — it declares the homeless, self-denying figures to be worth more than the world itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong: a canonical text exalting wilderness renunciants above the world; the Kural's insistence on disciplined conduct is implied in the passage rather than stated.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth easily, and when the ignorant address them [harshly], they say [words of] peace, And those who spend [part of] the night to their Lord prostrating and standing [in prayer]”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an's portrait of the ʿibād ar-Raḥmān, the servants of the Merciful, describes people marked by humility, gentleness under provocation, and night-long vigil rather than by worldly appetite.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, revealed scripture singles out the self-disciplined, desire-restraining person for its highest praise.
islam._accuracy_note: Honest gap: the Qur'an praises the humble, night-praying devotee rather than the world-renouncer, and elsewhere (57:27) is explicitly reserved about monasticism, so this is a close cousin rather than a twin.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Such is the way [of a life] of Torah: you shall eat bread with salt, and rationed water shall you drink; you shall sleep on the ground, your life will be one of privation, and in Torah shall you labor.”
judaism.explanation: The closing chapter of Pirkei Avot lays out deliberate material deprivation as the proper setting for a life devoted to Torah, and promises that such a life is blessed in this world and the next.
judaism.tie_back: A revered Jewish text setting austerity and discipline at the top of its scale of value, which is the Kural's exact claim about what books conclude.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 6:4 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close in substance — a canonical rabbinic text commending an ascetic regimen as the highest way; it prescribes the life rather than praising a class of people who already live it.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though month after month for a hundred years one should offer sacrifices by the thousands, yet if only for a moment one should worship those of perfected minds that honor is indeed better than a century of sacrifice.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada measures a lifetime of ritual offerings against a single instant of reverence for the perfected and finds the ritual wanting.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's thesis in Buddhist form: the settled verdict of the text is that honouring the renounced outranks every other meritorious thing.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: a canonical verse performing an explicit comparative ranking that puts reverence for the perfected renunciant above all rival goods.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Zeus turns his eyes away from the fighting at Troy to the northern peoples, among them the milk-drinking Hippemolgoi and the Abioi, whom Homer calls the most righteous of men — a people imagined as living without wealth, war or luxury.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek epic occasionally idealises distant peoples whose material simplicity is taken as proof of moral superiority to the acquisitive Greek world.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the nearest thing in Greek epic to the Kural's claim that the texts reserve their highest praise for those who own and want least.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak, and honestly so: these are an idealised foreign tribe, not chosen renunciants, and Homer's aside is two lines long — Greek myth simply has no established ascetic class to exalt.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus devotes a whole discourse to the Cynic vocation, describing the true Cynic as a man with no house, no property, no wife and nothing but his own body, whom Zeus sends into the world as a messenger and a scout to show other people where good and evil actually lie.
philosophy.explanation: For Epictetus the propertyless wanderer is not a social failure but the highest human office, because only someone who wants nothing can testify credibly about what is worth wanting.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, a teaching tradition places the disciplined renunciant at the summit of its own scale of human excellence.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match — an authoritative philosophical text ranking the renunciant highest; paraphrased rather than quoted because the discourse makes the point across many pages.

kurals.tamil:
துறந்தார் பெருமை துணைக்கூறின் வையத்து
இறந்தாரை எண்ணிக்கொண் டற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Thurandhaar perumai thunaikkoorin vaiyaththu,
Irandhaarai ennikkon datru.
kurals.meaning: To try to state how great those who have renounced are is like trying to count every person who has ever died on this earth.
kurals.elementary: Imagine someone asked you to count every leaf that has ever fallen from every tree in the world. You could start, but you could never finish. This kural says that asking “how great are people who have let go of wanting things?” is that same kind of question — too big to ever finish counting.
kurals.university: The force of the verse is in “thunaik-koorin” — “if one were to say the measure (thunai) of it.” Thunai here is quantity, extent, an amount; the couplet is not saying the renunciant's greatness is hard to describe but that it is the wrong sort of thing to put a number on. The chosen comparison is deliberately brutal: “vaiyaththu irandhaarai ennikkondu,” tallying up everyone who has ever died in the world, an arithmetic that is not merely large but principled endless, since the dead accumulate faster than any count. Commentators from Parimelazhagar onward read the simile as one of category error rather than mere magnitude. Placed second in the chapter, it functions as a rhetorical guard-rail: having just claimed in Kural 21 that the books rank renunciants highest, Valluvar immediately blocks the reader from imagining that this ranking could be cashed out in any scale or quantity.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Taittiriya Upanishad measures out a ladder of bliss, multiplying each rung a hundredfold from human joy up to the bliss of Brahman, and then breaks off its own arithmetic by saying that from that bliss words turn back, together with the mind, unable to reach it.
hinduism.explanation: The text deliberately starts an enumeration in order to demonstrate that enumeration fails: the highest state is reached by abandoning the measuring apparatus, not by extending it.
hinduism.tie_back: The same structure as the Kural — begin to count, then show that counting is the wrong instrument for this object.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong structural parallel (a failed measurement used as a proof of transcendence), but the Upanishad is measuring the bliss of Brahman rather than the greatness of renunciants; paraphrased because English renderings of 2.9 vary widely.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets:”
christianity.explanation: The writer of Hebrews abandons his own list of the faithful mid-sentence, conceding that the catalogue of the righteous outruns the time available to recite it.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, the text stages its own failure to enumerate as the strongest possible tribute to those it is praising.
christianity._accuracy_note: Good rhetorical match — an explicit refusal to finish counting the righteous; the impossibility here is practical (time fails) rather than the Kural's stronger claim of principled uncountability.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account [i.e., limit].”
islam.explanation: The closing clause of the verse promises the ṣābirūn — those who endure and hold back — a reward given bi-ghayri ḥisāb, without reckoning, outside the ordinary ledger of deeds and payments.
islam.tie_back: The Qur'an makes the same point about the self-restrained that the Kural makes about the renounced: their worth is explicitly taken off the accounting scale.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close — the phrase 'without account' is literally a refusal to quantify, applied to exactly the kind of person the Kural has in view; the Qur'an speaks of reward rather than of greatness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “These are the things that have no definite quantity: The corners [of the field]. First-fruits; [The offerings brought] on appearing [at the Temple on the three pilgrimage festivals]. The performance of righteous deeds; And the study of the torah.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah opens the tractate on gleanings by listing the obligations that Jewish law deliberately leaves without a fixed measure, so that no ceiling can be placed on them.
judaism.tie_back: A legal text formally declaring certain goods to be unquantifiable, which is exactly the move the Kural makes about the greatness of renunciants.
judaism.source: Mishnah Peah 1:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: The shared idea of 'things without measure' is genuine and unusual, but the Mishnah is defining unbounded obligations, not praising ascetics — a real but oblique correspondence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who reveres those worthy of reverence, the Buddhas and their disciples, who have transcended all obstacles and passed beyond the reach of sorrow and lamentation — he who reveres such peaceful and fearless ones, his merit none can compute by any measure.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says that even the by-product of honouring the perfected — the merit accruing to the one who honours them — defeats every attempt at calculation.
buddhism.tie_back: A near-verbatim parallel: the greatness attaching to the renounced is declared, in as many words, incomputable by any measure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: About as close as cross-tradition matching gets — same subject (the renounced), same predicate (immeasurability), same rhetorical shape.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Odysseus summons the dead at the edge of the world and they come up in such numbers, with such a cry, that he loses his nerve and flees back to his ship rather than face the countless tribes of the perished.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer uses the sheer unmanageable multitude of the dead as an image of something a living person cannot confront or take stock of.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It supplies the Kural's own comparison in narrative form — the dead of the world are the standing Greek image of a number no one can take.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The match is with the Kural's simile rather than its point: Homer gives a vivid picture of the uncountable dead, but says nothing about ascetics.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
philosophy.explanation: The final proposition of the Tractatus marks off a domain — value, ethics, the sense of the world — which Wittgenstein holds can be shown but never stated in propositions that measure facts.
philosophy.tie_back: It formalises the Kural's instinct that some kinds of greatness are not the sort of thing about which a measurement can be pronounced at all.
philosophy.source: Ludwig Wittgenstein, Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus, Proposition 7 (trans. C.K. Ogden, 1922)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Honestly a stretch: the shared idea is the limit of what can be stated or measured, but Wittgenstein is doing logic, not praising renunciants, and the resemblance is formal rather than substantive.

kurals.tamil:
இருமை வகைதெரிந்து ஈண்டுஅறம் பூண்டார்
பெருமை பிறங்கிற்று உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Irumai vakaitherindhu eendaram poondaar,
Perumai pirangitru ulagu.
kurals.meaning: Nothing shines higher in this world than the greatness of those who, having discerned the two orders of existence, have taken up the life of virtue here and now.
kurals.elementary: Some people look at two roads and can actually tell which one leads somewhere good and which one just looks fun for a little while. This kural says the people who can tell the difference — and then actually start walking the good road today, not someday — are the brightest people in the whole world.
kurals.university: “Irumai” — “twoness” — is the pivot, and the commentators do not agree on what the two are. Parimelazhagar takes them as this birth and the next (iham and param); Manakkudavar and several modern readers take them as birth and release from birth, the round of rebirth against liberation; a third reading makes them pleasure and good, the transient and the abiding. Valluvar leaves the ambiguity intact, which is characteristic: what matters is not which pair you name but that you have actually distinguished (“vakai therindhu,” sorted out the kinds) rather than drifted. Against that discernment he sets the sharply temporal “eendu” — here, in this place, in this life — so that the verse refuses to let the insight be postponed to a future existence. “Pirangitru” (from pirangu-, to shine forth, to be conspicuous) makes the resulting greatness visible in the world rather than hidden in it; the renunciant's virtue is not an inward secret but the brightest public fact the world contains.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end.”
hinduism.explanation: Death himself teaches Nachiketas that the preyas (the pleasant) and the shreyas (the good) present themselves together, and that everything depends on being able to tell them apart before choosing.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's “irumai vakai therindhu” almost word for word: discerning the two kinds, then binding oneself to the better one.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.2.1-2 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong: both texts make discernment between a paired alternative the decisive act, and both attach the ascetic's greatness to having made the harder choice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.”
christianity.explanation: Paul contrasts two orders of reality — the visible and passing against the invisible and lasting — and says the Christian's whole orientation follows from keeping that distinction in view.
christianity.tie_back: Same structure as the Kural: two kinds are distinguished, and greatness lies in ordering one's present life by that distinction.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on the two-orders structure and on acting in the present in light of it; Paul does not single out a renunciant class the way the Kural does.

islam.quote_or_event: “But you prefer the worldly life, While the Hereafter is better and more enduring.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an rebukes the human habit of choosing the immediate over the lasting, and names the two options plainly so that the choice cannot be made in ignorance.
islam.tie_back: The verse presents exactly the two kinds the Kural says the great have discerned, and identifies which one the wise take up.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong: the paired this-world/hereafter framing is the same, and the verse's whole point is that the two must be told apart and ranked correctly.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Jacob said: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come; prepare yourself in the vestibule, so that you may enter the banqueting-hall.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah's image makes the present world real but preliminary, and makes preparation in the here and now the only access to what follows.
judaism.tie_back: Both the two-order distinction and the Kural's insistence on “eendu,” acting here rather than later, are present in a single sentence.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:16 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Unusually close: the two-world scheme plus the urgency of preparing in this life map onto both halves of the couplet.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Lead a righteous life; lead not a base life. The righteous live happily both in this world and the next.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's chapter on the world sets the two possible ways of living side by side and reports the outcome across both existences.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes the choice of dharma here the thing that determines standing in both orders of existence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on the two-worlds framing and on taking up virtue now; the verse is addressed to everyone rather than to renunciants specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plato closes the Republic with the myth of Er, a soldier who dies, travels to the place where souls are judged and choose their next lives, and returns to tell the living what he saw — the point of the account being that a person who has seen both worlds will choose the just life rather than the merely attractive one.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story is designed to give the reader the vantage point of someone who has surveyed both existences at once, so that the choice between them can be made knowingly.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises exactly the Kural's claim that greatness begins with having actually discerned the two orders, not merely heard of them.
greek_mythology.source: Plato, Republic X (the Myth of Er, 614b-621d)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A genuine Greek narrative about knowing both worlds and choosing accordingly, but it is a philosopher's constructed myth rather than traditional mythology, and it centres on justice rather than renunciation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For I deem that the true disciple of philosophy is likely to be misunderstood by other men; they do not perceive that he is ever pursuing death and dying.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates argues on his last day that philosophy just is the practice of separating oneself from the body's demands, so that the philosopher has been rehearsing for the other order of existence all along.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural's renunciant, the philosopher is great precisely because he has taken the measure of both states and arranged his present life around the better one.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong: an ascetic practice justified explicitly by knowledge of two states of being; the Greek framing is about the soul's separation rather than about release from rebirth.

kurals.tamil:
உரனென்னும் தோட்டியான் ஓரைந்தும் காப்பான்
வரனென்னும் வைப்பிற்கோர் வித்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Uranennum thottiyaan oraindhum kaappaan,
Varanennum vaippirkor viththu.
kurals.meaning: The one who holds all five senses in check with the goad called firmness of mind is a seed for that highest of all estates, liberation.
kurals.elementary: A person riding a huge elephant carries a small hooked stick, and with that one little stick they can steer an animal far stronger than they are. This kural says your five senses are like five elephants, and a steady mind is the little hook that steers them — and steering them is how something wonderful gets planted.
kurals.university: The image is precise and technical: “thotti” is the ankusa, the mahout's hooked goad, and the “oraindhu,” the five, are the sense-faculties imagined as five rutting elephants. Against their bulk Valluvar sets “uran,” mental firmness or resolve — the smallest instrument mastering the largest force, which is the whole argument of the verse in one picture. The payoff clause is theologically loaded: “varan” (from Sanskrit vara, the choicest) names the supreme estate, and “vaippu” is a deposit or treasure-store, so the ascetic becomes “or viththu,” a single seed, for that store. The seed metaphor matters — the sense-controller is not said to have arrived, but to be the germ from which the highest state grows, which keeps the emphasis on practice rather than attainment. The Tamil Shaiva tradition heard this verse as close kin to Tirumular's Tirumandiram, which likewise sets the goad of knowledge against the elephants of the senses.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins. The senses they call the horses, the objects of the senses their roads.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad's chariot allegory assigns each part of the person a role in a single vehicle, and makes everything depend on whether the driver holds the reins firmly enough to control the animals.
hinduism.tie_back: The same claim with a different draught animal: a small instrument of resolve governing the powerful senses is what carries a person to the highest place.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.3-4 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong — same structure (senses as animals, discipline as the controlling instrument, liberation as the destination); horses and reins rather than elephants and a goad.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.”
christianity.explanation: Paul borrows the vocabulary of athletic training to describe a deliberate, forcible mastery of his own appetites, undertaken because he does not consider himself exempt from failing.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats bodily self-restraint not as an optional austerity but as the very condition of reaching the prize.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the substance of forcible sense-restraint aimed at a final reward; Paul speaks of the body generally rather than enumerating five faculties.

islam.quote_or_event: “But as for he who feared the position of his Lord and prevented the soul from [unlawful] inclination, Then indeed, Paradise will be [his] refuge.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an sets out a two-step condition — reverent awareness, then active restraint of the soul's appetite — and attaches Paradise directly to it.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's causal chain exactly: restraint of appetite now is what makes the highest estate one's destination.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: restraint of the nafs is named as the precondition and Paradise as the consequence, matching the 'seed for the highest estate' structure.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who is mighty? He who subdues his [evil] inclination, as it is said: ‘He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that rules his spirit than he that takes a city’ (Proverbs 16:32).”
judaism.explanation: Ben Zoma redefines strength itself: real power is not what a person can do to the world but what a person can do to the yetzer, the appetitive drive inside.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts locate the decisive strength in the small inner instrument that governs appetite, not in outward force.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 4:1 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong on the inner-mastery-as-true-power theme and on the paradox of the smaller force governing the greater; the yetzer is a single drive rather than five sense-channels.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Formerly this mind wandered about as it liked, where it wished and according to its pleasure, but now I shall thoroughly master it with wisdom as a mahout controls with his ankus an elephant in rut.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's Elephant chapter pictures the untrained mind as a musth elephant and wisdom as the mahout's hooked goad that brings it under control.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's exact image — goad, rutting elephant, faculty of restraint — appears here in an independent tradition.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Outstanding match: the ankus-and-elephant metaphor is shared almost verbatim; the Dhammapada applies it to the mind while the Kural applies it to the five senses.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Warned by Circe, Odysseus has his crew stop their ears with wax and orders them to lash him upright to the mast and to tighten the ropes if he begs to be freed, so that he can hear the Sirens' song and survive it.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus does not try to resist the pull of sensory pleasure by willpower in the moment; he binds his future self in advance, using a deliberate physical restraint as a substitute for restraint of desire.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the Greek world's clearest picture of the Kural's claim that a deliberate instrument of restraint applied to the senses is what saves a person.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Genuinely close on sense-restraint as the saving act; the difference is that Odysseus restrains himself externally with ropes rather than internally with firmness of mind.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.”
philosophy.explanation: In Plato's allegory the soul is a chariot whose driver, reason, must control an obedient horse and an unruly appetitive one if the soul is to rise toward the truth.
philosophy.tie_back: Same claim as the Kural: the ascent to the highest state depends on a governing faculty keeping the appetitive powers in hand.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very strong and historically striking — Max Müller himself noted the resemblance between this passage and the Katha Upanishad's chariot; the appetitive powers are two horses rather than five senses.

kurals.tamil:
ஐந்தவித்தான் ஆற்றல் அகல்விசும்பு ளார்கோமான்
இந்திரனே சாலுங் கரி.
kurals.transliteration:
Aindhaviththaan aatral akalvisumbu ulaarkoman,
Indhirane saalung kari.
kurals.meaning: Indra himself, lord of the dwellers in the wide heavens, is proof enough of the power of the one who has extinguished the desires of all five senses.
kurals.elementary: Imagine the strongest king in the world admitting that someone else is stronger than him. That would settle the argument, wouldn't it? This kural says the king of the sky-world himself is the living proof of how powerful a person becomes when they put out the fire of wanting.
kurals.university: “Aindhavith-thaan” is built on avi-, to extinguish or quench, so the ascetic has not merely restrained the five but put them out, as one puts out a lamp. Against this Valluvar sets a legal metaphor: Indra, “akal visumbu ulaar koman,” king of those in the wide sky, is the “kari” — the witness, the one whose testimony settles a case. The choice of Indra is doubly pointed. In Puranic narrative Indra's own sovereignty was won by tapas, so his throne is itself an exhibit of what austerity produces; and Indra is famously the god who panics when a human ascetic's penance grows strong enough to threaten his seat, which makes his testimony that of a reluctant expert witness. Some commentators, including Parimelazhagar, also read a darker allusion to the Ahalya episode, in which Indra's own failure to quench desire cost him everything — in which case the god testifies not by his glory but by his fall. Notably, the Kural cites Indra only as evidence, never as an object of worship.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Ramayana's account of Vishvamitra, the king-turned-ascetic's austerities grow so formidable that Indra, fearing for his own throne, sends the apsara Menaka to break the sage's concentration — and the heavenly court's alarm becomes the measure of what the ascetic had achieved.
hinduism.explanation: The recurring Puranic pattern is that the gods intervene against human tapas not out of malice but out of well-founded fear: accumulated austerity is a real force that can rival theirs.
hinduism.tie_back: This is precisely the Kural's evidentiary move — Indra's own conduct is what proves the power of the man who has quenched the five.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (the Vishvamitra and Menaka episode, sargas 63-64)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong: this is almost certainly the body of story Valluvar is gesturing at, and Indra's fear functions exactly as the 'sufficient witness' the couplet names.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus explains his disciples' failure to cast out a spirit by pointing to a power that only sustained prayer and fasting confer — asceticism is presented as producing real, verifiable capacity.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats ascetic self-denial as the source of a demonstrable power rather than as mere piety.
christianity._accuracy_note: Solid on the core idea that fasting confers power, but the Christian text supplies no heavenly witness testifying to that power, which is the Kural's distinctive framing.

islam.quote_or_event: “By Him in Whose Hands my soul is, the smell coming out from the mouth of a fasting person is better in the sight of Allah than the smell of musk. (Allah says about the fasting person), ‘He has left his food, drink and desires for My sake. The fast is for Me. So I will reward (the fasting person) for it and the reward of good deeds is multiplied ten times.’”
islam.explanation: In this hadith God Himself speaks about the faster, claiming the fast as His own and declaring that the physical evidence of hunger is more pleasing to Him than perfume.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, it is the highest authority in the heavens who furnishes the testimony about what self-denial is worth.
islam._accuracy_note: The heavenly-testimony structure matches well, but the hadith attests to the fast's acceptability rather than to the ascetic's power, which is the Kural's actual subject.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud reports that a heavenly voice went out each day declaring that the whole world is sustained on account of Hanina ben Dosa — a sage so poor that he lived on a measure of carob pods from one Sabbath eve to the next.
judaism.explanation: The passage deliberately juxtaposes extreme material deprivation with cosmic significance, and puts the assessment in the mouth of a voice from heaven rather than of admiring humans.
judaism.tie_back: A heavenly authority testifying to the power of a man who has renounced appetite is the Kural's exact structure.
judaism._accuracy_note: Structurally very close — heavenly witness, ascetic subject, claim of world-sustaining power; paraphrased rather than quoted because English renderings differ and I did not verify one word for word.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Even the gods hold dear the wise one, whose senses are subdued like horses well trained by a charioteer, whose pride is destroyed and who is free from the cankers.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's chapter on the perfected states plainly that the arahant's standing is recognised by the devas themselves, who occupy a lower rung than the liberated human.
buddhism.tie_back: Same claim, same witnesses: the gods' regard is offered as the proof of what sense-mastery accomplishes.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent: subdued senses, divine beings as the attesting party, and the implicit ranking of the liberated human above the gods all line up with the couplet.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles, after a life of imposed labours and endurance, is burned free of his mortal part on Mount Oeta and taken up to Olympus, where the gods who had set him his trials receive him as one of their own.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek myth's one clear case of a human ascending to divine rank makes endurance and hardship, rather than birth, the qualification — and the Olympians' acceptance is what certifies it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Indra's testimony in the Kural, the divine court's own recognition is what establishes that a human being's self-conquest has reached superhuman force.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fair rather than strong: the divine-certification structure is genuine, but Heracles endures labours imposed on him rather than quenching desire, and he is anything but continent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Alexander the Great, at the height of his power, sought out Diogenes the Cynic sunning himself and asked what he could do for him; Diogenes asked him only to stop blocking the sun, and Alexander afterwards told his companions that if he were not Alexander he would wish to be Diogenes.
philosophy.explanation: The most powerful man in the world publicly concedes that the man who owns nothing occupies the more enviable position, and the concession is what gives the anecdote its force.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's evidentiary logic transposed to the human plane: the king himself is the sufficient witness to the ascetic's superior power.
philosophy.source: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 14; cf. Diogenes Laertius 6.32
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the crucial point — the highest worldly authority testifying to the renunciant's greater power; paraphrased because the wording varies between Plutarch and Diogenes Laertius.

kurals.tamil:
செயற்கரிய செய்வார் பெரியர் சிறியர்
செயற்கரிய செய்கலா தார்.
kurals.transliteration:
Seyarkariya seyvaar periyar siriyar,
Seyarkariya seykalaa thaar.
kurals.meaning: The great are those who do what is hard to do; the small are those who cannot do what is hard to do.
kurals.elementary: Two people stand in front of the same steep hill. One starts climbing even though it hurts; the other says “too hard” and walks away. This kural says that is the whole difference between a big person and a small one — not how they look, just which one starts climbing.
kurals.university: The couplet is built as a chiasmus, with “seyarkariya” (things difficult to do) standing at the head of both halves so that the same object divides humanity into two classes. What is striking is the definition's austerity: Valluvar offers no content for greatness at all, no list of virtues, only a functional test. “Periyar” and “siriyar” — the great and the small — are terms he uses throughout the Kural as a moral rather than a social ranking, and here he strips them of every birth-based or wealth-based criterion. In context the difficult things are the ascetic disciplines named in the surrounding verses: quenching the senses, discerning the two worlds, holding anger. Later Tamil tradition, reading the chapter alongside yogic literature, glossed the “hard things” as the eight limbs of yoga from yama through samadhi. The verse's blunt symmetry has made it one of the most-quoted couplets in Tamil, routinely cited well outside any ascetic context.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard.”
hinduism.explanation: The Katha Upanishad refuses to soften the demand: the road to self-knowledge is compared to walking a razor's edge, and the hearer is roused rather than comforted.
hinduism.tie_back: It supplies exactly what the Kural leaves implicit — that the thing which separates the great from the small is a path most people will not attempt because it is hard.
hinduism.source: Katha Upanishad 1.3.14 (trans. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong on the shared premise that difficulty is the defining feature of the highest path; the Upanishad urges the effort rather than classifying people by it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But Jesus beheld them, and said unto them, With men this is impossible; but with God all things are possible.”
christianity.explanation: The disciples have just watched a wealthy man refuse the demand to sell everything and follow, and they ask in astonishment who then can be saved; Jesus concedes the difficulty outright before answering it.
christianity.tie_back: The passage stages the Kural's division exactly — one man finds the hard thing undoable and walks away, and the difficulty is named as the whole issue.
christianity._accuracy_note: The narrative setting (a renunciation too hard to perform) matches well, though Jesus resolves the difficulty by referring it to divine power rather than by grading people as great or small.

islam.quote_or_event: “The Paradise is surrounded by hardships and the Hell-Fire is surrounded by temptations.”
islam.explanation: The hadith pictures the two destinations as walled in by what stands in front of them: to reach Paradise one must push through what is unpleasant, while what is pleasant leads the other way.
islam.tie_back: It gives the Kural's criterion a topography — doing the hard thing is literally the only route, and failing to do it is what defines the lesser path.
islam._accuracy_note: Close on substance: difficulty as the marker of the higher road, ease as the marker of the lower; it rates destinations rather than persons.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ben Hei Hei's maxim in Pirkei Avot, l'fum tza'ara agra, teaches that the reward is in proportion to the difficulty — the harder the exertion a mitzvah demands, the greater what is earned by it.
judaism.explanation: The rabbinic principle turns difficulty into a measure of value rather than a reason for exemption, so effort itself becomes the unit of account.
judaism.tie_back: Both sayings make the capacity to shoulder what is hard the index of a person's standing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Honest partial match — the equation of difficulty with worth is shared, but the Mishnah measures reward rather than sorting people into the great and the small; paraphrased because I did not verify a single English rendering word for word.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he indeed is the noblest victor who conquers himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada sets the hardest available achievement — self-conquest — above the most spectacular external one, and awards greatness accordingly.
buddhism.tie_back: Same verdict as the Kural: the title of 'great' goes to whoever can do the thing that is genuinely difficult to do.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong: both verses rank people by difficulty of achievement, and the Dhammapada names the specific hard thing the Kural's chapter has in view.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Heracles is set twelve labours that no other man could survive — strangling the Nemean lion whose hide no weapon can pierce, fetching Cerberus out of the underworld — and his standing in Greek myth rests entirely on his having completed tasks designed to be impossible.
greek_mythology.explanation: The labours are explicitly chosen for their undoability; the hero's greatness is constituted by the doing of them rather than demonstrated by anything else.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth's central definition of a great man is the Kural's definition: the one who does what cannot be done.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Genuinely close on the criterion of greatness, though the labours are feats of strength and endurance rather than the inward ascetic difficulty the chapter is about.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “…it is no easy task to be good. For in everything it is no easy task to find the middle… to do this to the right person, to the right extent, at the right time, with the right motive, and in the right way, that is not for every one, nor is it easy; wherefore goodness is both rare and laudable and noble.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle argues that virtue consists in hitting a mean that is difficult to locate and harder to hit reliably, and concludes that this difficulty is exactly why goodness is rare and admirable.
philosophy.tie_back: He reaches the Kural's conclusion by analysis: it is the difficulty of the thing that makes those who manage it great, and its rarity that makes most people small.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics II.9, 1109a24-30 (trans. W.D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong philosophical parallel linking difficulty, rarity and praiseworthiness; Aristotle's hard thing is hitting the mean rather than renouncing the world.

kurals.tamil:
சுவைஒளி ஊறுஓசை நாற்றமென்று ஐந்தின்
வகைதெரிவான் கட்டே உலகு.
kurals.transliteration:
Suvaiyoli oorosai naatramendru aindhin,
Vakaitherivaan katte ulagu.
kurals.meaning: The world lies within the grasp of the one who has thoroughly understood the nature of the five — taste, sight, touch, sound and smell.
kurals.elementary: Everything you know about the world came in through five doors: what you taste, see, feel, hear and smell. This kural says the person who really understands those five doors — how they work and how they fool you — is the one who has the whole world figured out.
kurals.university: Valluvar lists the five not as organs but as their objects — suvai (taste), oli (light or form), ooru (touch), osai (sound), naatram (smell) — which is the classical Indian tanmatra scheme, each sense-object paired with one of the five elements. The operative phrase is “vakai therivaan,” the one who discerns the kinds, and “kattu” means a bond, a grip, or a thing held fast: the world is in his hold. Commentators split productively here. Parimelazhagar reads it epistemically — the one who analyses the sense-modes comprehends the world, since the world is nothing but what arrives through them. Others, including modern commentators like Salomon Pappaiah, read it practically — the one who has severed the desires arising through the five has the world at his command. Both readings depend on the same underlying premise, which is arrestingly close to later phenomenology: the world is not encountered apart from the five channels, so mastery of the channels is mastery of the world.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “O son of Kuntī, the nonpermanent appearance of happiness and distress, and their disappearance in due course, are like the appearance and disappearance of winter and summer seasons. They arise from sense perception, O scion of Bharata, and one must learn to tolerate them without being disturbed.”
hinduism.explanation: The Sanskrit phrase Krishna uses, mātrā-sparśāḥ, means literally the contacts of the sense-measures — he is telling Arjuna that pleasure and pain are just the coming and going of sense-contact, and that knowing this is what makes them bearable.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses hold that understanding the nature of the five sense-channels is what puts a person on top of experience rather than underneath it.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good on the shared premise that the sense-contacts are the raw material of experience and that discerning their nature confers mastery; the Gita's conclusion is endurance rather than possession of the world.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.”
christianity.explanation: John analyses 'the world' into a short taxonomy of appetites, treating it not as a place but as a set of channels through which desire operates on a person.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it identifies the world with what comes in through the senses, and makes knowing that taxonomy the first step to not being ruled by it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Real but partial: the move of defining 'the world' as sense-appetite is shared, yet John lists three categories rather than five and urges renunciation rather than discernment.

islam.quote_or_event: “And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an makes the sense-faculties themselves accountable, treating hearing and sight as agents that will be interrogated rather than as neutral instruments.
islam.tie_back: Both verses take the sense-channels as the decisive site of a person's relation to the world, and make knowledge of them the governing requirement.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong: the verse enumerates sense-faculties and ties them directly to knowledge and responsibility, closely paralleling the Kural's epistemic framing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And it shall be unto you for a fringe, that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them; and that ye seek not after your own heart and your own eyes, after which ye use to go a whoring:”
judaism.explanation: The Torah's command of the tzitzit works by installing a counter-sign in the visual field itself, on the explicit reasoning that the eyes and the heart lead a person astray by their own momentum.
judaism.tie_back: It rests on the Kural's premise that the senses are the channel through which the world takes hold of a person, so the remedy has to be applied at that channel.
judaism._accuracy_note: Moderate: shares the diagnosis that the senses drive the self, but prescribes an external reminder rather than the analytical discernment the Kural praises, and it names two faculties rather than five.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What is the All? Simply the eye & forms, ear & sounds, nose & aromas, tongue & flavors, body & tactile sensations, intellect & ideas. This, monks, is called the All. Anyone who would say, ‘Repudiating this All, I will describe another,’ … would be unable to explain, and furthermore, would be put to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha defines the totality of what there is exhaustively in terms of the sense-bases and their objects, and rules out in advance any 'world' lying outside them.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's claim made into doctrine: the world simply is the field of the sense-channels, so the one who has discerned them has the world.
buddhism.source: Sabba Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 35.23 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Excellent: an explicit identification of the world with the sense-fields, which is exactly the premise the Kural relies on; Buddhism counts six bases by including the mind.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Circe turns Odysseus' crew into swine by way of food and drink; Odysseus alone walks into her hall unharmed because Hermes has given him the herb moly and told him the nature of her drugs in advance, so he drinks and is not transformed.
greek_mythology.explanation: The crew are undone by sensory pleasure taken without understanding, while Odysseus meets the same pleasure with prior knowledge of what it is and passes through it intact.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It dramatises the Kural's point that it is knowing the nature of sense-experience, not avoiding it, that leaves a person in command.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A fair thematic echo — knowledge of sensory danger as protection — but Homer supplies a magic herb rather than analytic discernment, and there is no enumeration of five senses.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus separates the raw sense-impression from the judgement a person adds to it, and locates all disturbance in the second, which is the part within our power.
philosophy.tie_back: Like the Kural, it makes analysis of how impressions reach us the lever by which a person stops being at the world's mercy.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Genuine but partial: Stoic analysis of impressions parallels the Kural's discernment of sense-modes, though Epictetus focuses on judgement rather than on the five channels themselves.

kurals.tamil:
நிறைமொழி மாந்தர் பெருமை நிலத்து
மறைமொழி காட்டி விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Niraimozhi maandhar perumai nilaththu,
Maraimozhi kaatti vidum.
kurals.meaning: The greatness of those whose words carry their full power is made plain on earth by the sacred sayings they have left behind.
kurals.elementary: Some people say things that just stay true, long after they have gone — you can still hear them repeated hundreds of years later. This kural says you do not need to have met such a person to know how great they were; the words they left behind tell you.
kurals.university: The couplet turns on a pair of near-rhyming compounds. “Nirai-mozhi” is full speech — words so complete that what they say comes about; “marai-mozhi” is hidden or sacred speech, the mantra, the word set apart. Valluvar's claim is evidential: the greatness of such people is not something we take on trust but something the surviving sayings “kaatti vidum,” show up, display, on the earth (“nilaththu”). The verse encodes an old South Asian doctrine of the efficacious utterance — the satya-vakya or act of truth, in which a perfected person's word alters reality because it proceeds from a life that contains no falsehood. What is distinctly Valluvar's is the inversion: rather than arguing that great people produce powerful words, he argues from the words back to the people, making the surviving text the standing proof. The line has an obvious reflexivity for a reader holding the Kural itself, and Tamil tradition has not missed it.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vedic tradition holds that the hymns were not composed but seen — each sukta is assigned to a named rishi who is its mantra-drashta, its seer — so that the surviving mantra is the standing evidence of the seer's realisation, and the anukramani indexes preserve those names alongside the verses.
hinduism.explanation: In this framework the sage does not own the mantra and the mantra does not flatter the sage; the relationship is evidential, with the enduring efficacious word testifying to the state of the one who saw it.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact logic — the sacred saying left on earth is what displays the greatness of the person of full speech.
hinduism.source: Rig Veda and the rishi-attribution tradition of the Sarvanukramani
hinduism._accuracy_note: Conceptually very close, and probably part of the intellectual background Valluvar assumes; described as a tradition rather than quoted because it is a framework spread across texts rather than a single citable line.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus claims a durability for his sayings greater than that of the physical cosmos, making the words rather than any monument the lasting evidence of who spoke them.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats surviving speech as the thing that carries a person's greatness forward into the world.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the endurance of the sacred word as the mark of the speaker; it asserts the words' permanence rather than using them as evidence of the speaker's greatness.

islam.quote_or_event: “Many a person with disheveled hair and covered with dust is turned away from the doors (whereas he is held in such a high esteem by Allah) that if he were to adjure in the name of Allah (about anything) Allah would fulfil that.”
islam.explanation: The hadith describes a person whose outward appearance invites contempt but whose word, sworn before God, is honoured — his unregarded speech is the exact index of his standing.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural's doctrine of full speech: the word of the renunciant is effective, and its effectiveness is what reveals a greatness the world had missed.
islam.source: Sahih Muslim 2622 (Book of Virtue, chapter on the virtue of the weak and downtrodden)
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent match: a dusty, propertyless ascetic whose oath God fulfils is precisely the 'man of full speech' the couplet has in view.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud draws from a verse about one who rules over people justly the astonishing corollary that the righteous rule over the fear of God: God decrees and the tzaddik may annul the decree.
judaism.explanation: The rabbis take the efficacy of a righteous person's word to such a limit that it is said to override heaven's own pronouncement, making speech the visible measure of sanctity.
judaism.tie_back: Both traditions read a holy person's greatness directly off the power their words are found to carry.
judaism._accuracy_note: Substantively very close on the efficacious word of the righteous; paraphrased rather than quoted because I did not verify a specific English translation word for word.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Sent to help a woman in obstructed labour, the former bandit Angulimala performs an act of truth, declaring that since he was born in the noble birth he has never intentionally taken a life — and on the strength of that true statement the woman and her child are delivered safely.
buddhism.explanation: The saccakiriya works only because the statement is true of the speaker; the power belongs not to the formula but to the life that can say it without falsehood.
buddhism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural's claim — the efficacy of the surviving utterance is what discloses what kind of person stood behind it.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very strong: the act of truth is the canonical Buddhist form of 'full speech' whose power certifies the speaker; paraphrased because the episode is a narrative rather than a line.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Tiresias, the blind Theban seer, is the one figure in Greek myth whose pronouncements always prove true — Oedipus rages at him and disbelieves him, and every word he has spoken comes about regardless, while he alone among the dead retains his mind and prophesies to Odysseus in the underworld.
greek_mythology.explanation: Greek tradition marks out the seer precisely by the fact that his speech is not opinion but something that happens, and his standing is established retrospectively by the fulfilment of his words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: As in the Kural, the greatness of the man is displayed by the words rather than the words by the man.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 300-462; cf. Homer, Odyssey 11.90-151
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Fair: the efficacious-word-proving-the-speaker structure is genuinely there, but Tiresias' authority comes from prophetic gift rather than from ascetic perfection of life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And the Sibyl, with raving lips uttering things mirthless, unbedizened, and unperfumed, reaches over a thousand years with her voice, thanks to the god in her.”
philosophy.explanation: Heraclitus contrasts the Sibyl's unadorned, unattractive speech with its reach, arguing that her words outlast a millennium precisely because they carry something other than ornament.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural's point in a single sentence: the plain sacred utterance persists, and its persistence is what testifies to the one who spoke it.
philosophy.source: Heraclitus, Fragment DK B92 (trans. John Burnet)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the enduring unadorned word as the evidence of an inspired speaker; Heraclitus credits the god in her rather than ascetic attainment.

kurals.tamil:
குணமென்னும் குன்றேறி நின்றார் வெகுளி
கணமேயும் காத்தல் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Gunamennum kundreri nindraar veguli,
Kanameyum kaaththal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: If those who stand on the hill called good character are once roused to anger, the person who provoked them can scarcely be shielded even for an instant.
kurals.elementary: Some people almost never get angry — so if one of them finally does, you know something has gone very wrong. This kural says the anger of a truly good person is like that: rare, and so serious that nobody can protect whoever caused it, not even for a second.
kurals.university: The couplet works by compounding two improbabilities. “Gunam-ennum kundru” — the hill called character — puts the sage at an elevation, and “nindraar,” having stood, stresses that he has held the position; such a person's “veguli,” hot anger, is by definition rare. Against that rarity Valluvar sets “kanam,” the blink of an eye, the smallest unit of Tamil time-reckoning, and the verb “kaaththal,” to guard or protect: even for a kanam the offender cannot be guarded. Commentators read the verse in two compatible ways — as a warning about the objective force of an ascetic's curse, a commonplace of Indian narrative, and as a moral observation that the anger of the habitually gentle is uniquely devastating because it can only mean a real wrong has been done. The verse is also a fine example of Valluvar's economy with sound: gunam / kundru and kanam / kaaththal set up internal echoes that make the couplet memorable in recitation.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Indra, riding his elephant, treats a garland given to him by the sage Durvasa with contempt and lets it be trampled, the sage curses him on the spot; the gods immediately lose their splendour and their sovereignty, and only the vast labour of churning the ocean for the nectar restores them.
hinduism.explanation: A single moment's disrespect toward an ascetic costs the king of the gods his kingdom, and no power in the three worlds can shield him from the consequence once the word is spoken.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural's warning in narrative form: no one, not even Indra, can be protected for an instant from a sage's roused anger.
hinduism.source: Bhagavata Purana 8.5-8 (the curse of Durvasa and the churning of the ocean)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong — the ascetic's momentary wrath producing instant, unstoppable ruin is exactly the couplet's claim, and this genre of story is almost certainly its background.

christianity.quote_or_event: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell property, secretly hold back part of the price, and lie about it to the apostles; Peter confronts each of them in turn, and each falls down dead at his words, so that great fear comes on the whole church.
christianity.explanation: The narrative gives no interval for appeal or protection — the apostle's rebuke and the consequence arrive together, and the community's reaction is fear rather than dispute.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, the offender against a holy man's integrity cannot be shielded even briefly once the sentence is spoken.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on the instant, unavoidable consequence of offending a holy figure; the text presents it as divine judgement rather than as the holy man's anger, which is a real difference.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah said, ‘I will declare war against him who shows hostility to a pious worshipper of Mine.’”
islam.explanation: This hadith qudsi opens by putting God Himself on the side of the devoted servant, framing hostility toward such a person not as a private quarrel but as a declaration of war with heaven.
islam.tie_back: It states the Kural's warning at maximum force: whoever provokes a person of realised piety is beyond anyone's protection.
islam.source: Sahih al-Bukhari 6502 (Book of Ar-Riqaq, chapter on humility)
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent: same content (offending the saintly person is catastrophic and unshieldable), though the agency is God's rather than the wali's own anger.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And [he also said:] warm yourself before the fire of the wise, but beware of being singed by their glowing coals, for their bite is the bite of a fox, and their sting is the sting of a scorpion, and their hiss is the hiss of a serpent, and all their words are like coals of fire.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Eliezer urges closeness to the sages and in the same breath warns that the same heat which warms can burn, cataloguing the danger in escalating animal images.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural's exact caution — the roused anger of a person of high character is a thing from which no one can be safely protected.
judaism.source: Pirkei Avot 2:10 (Mishnah Yomit, trans. Dr. Joshua Kulp)
judaism._accuracy_note: Outstanding: an ancient wisdom text explicitly warning that the anger of the virtuous wise is dangerous beyond remedy — the closest parallel in this chapter.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “One should not strike a holy man, nor should a holy man, when struck, give way to anger. Shame on him who strikes a holy man, and more shame on him who gives way to anger.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada protects the holy man from assault and in the same verse denies him the right to retaliate in anger, holding him to the higher standard precisely because of his attainment.
buddhism.tie_back: It addresses the Kural's situation and deliberately takes the other side: offending the holy is wrong, but the holy person's anger is a fault rather than a force.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Honestly a weak match, and interestingly so: Buddhism has no equivalent of the destructive sage's curse, so the closest canonical verse is one that contradicts the Kural's premise rather than supporting it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Chryses, priest of Apollo, is insulted and driven off by Agamemnon when he comes to ransom his daughter; he walks along the shore, prays once to his god, and Apollo comes down in anger and shoots a plague into the Greek camp that burns for nine days until the army is forced to submit.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Iliad opens with this episode precisely to show that slighting a holy man is not a social misstep but a catastrophe, and that the whole army cannot be shielded from the consequence of one man's arrogance.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's claim, dramatised: the offender and everyone near him are defenceless the moment a holy man's anger is provoked.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Very strong — one of the clearest cross-cultural instances of the offended-holy-man motif, with the same instantaneous and unstoppable outcome.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca argues at length in De Ira that anger is not a useful tool that a good person may occasionally deploy but a temporary madness that no one of genuine virtue would consent to entertain even briefly, and that the truly wise man therefore does not become angry at all.
philosophy.explanation: Stoicism treats freedom from anger as constitutive of the sage, so the notion of a virtuous person's wrath carrying moral authority is ruled out from the start.
philosophy.tie_back: It engages the Kural's subject directly and rejects its premise: for Seneca, a person standing on the hill of character does not get angry, so there is nothing to be shielded from.
philosophy.source: Seneca, De Ira (On Anger), esp. I.1 and III.5
philosophy._accuracy_note: Deliberately a low-confidence, contrastive entry — Greco-Roman philosophy has no doctrine of the efficacious wrath of the holy, and the nearest sustained treatment denies the phenomenon exists.

kurals.tamil:
அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர்மற் றெவ்வுயிர்க்கும்
செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுக லான்.
kurals.transliteration:
Andhanar enbor aravormatru evvuyirkkum,
Sendhanmai poondozhuga laan.
kurals.meaning: Those properly called anthanar are the truly virtuous, because they live wearing an unbroken, gracious compassion toward every living thing.
kurals.elementary: People sometimes think you are important because of the family you were born into. This kural says no: the title of the highest kind of person belongs to whoever treats every living creature — people, animals, everything — with real kindness, all the time.
kurals.university: The chapter's last couplet is also its most socially radical. “Anthanar,” the honorific ordinarily applied to Brahmins, is here redefined by conduct alone: anthanar are “aravor,” the virtuous, and the reason given is grammatical rather than incidental — the whole second line is a causal clause ending in “ozhuga-laan,” because they conduct themselves so. Traditional Tamil etymology reads anthanar as am (beautiful, gracious) + thanmai (coolness), and Valluvar exploits this by giving them “sen-thanmai,” upright or true coolness, a quality of unheated, unfailing graciousness extended to “ev-uyirkkum,” every living thing without exception — a phrase that takes the claim past human society and into the treatment of animals. Nothing about birth, ritual, thread or learning appears. The verse anchors the ahimsa ethic that Valluvar develops at length in the later chapters on compassion (Arul-udaimai) and abstaining from meat (Pulaal maruththal), and it has been a central text in modern Tamil arguments against caste, including in the work of the twentieth-century reform movements.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The humble sages, by virtue of true knowledge, see with equal vision a learned and gentle brāhmaṇa, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater [outcaste].”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna's list is constructed to cross every boundary at once — caste, species, and ritual purity — and to say that real knowledge dissolves the distinction between them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both verses redefine the brahmin by a levelling regard for all living beings rather than by birth or rank.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 5.18 (Bhagavad-gītā As It Is, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupāda)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very strong: the brāhmaṇa, animals and the outcaste appear in one breath, matching the Kural's 'every living thing' and its detachment of status from birth.

christianity.quote_or_event: Francis of Assisi, having given away his property, is remembered in the early lives for preaching to a flock of birds by the roadside, addressing them as his sisters and urging them to praise their creator, and for treating wolf, lamb and leper alike as creatures owed courtesy.
christianity.explanation: The Franciscan tradition made the extension of charity beyond humanity to animals and the whole created order the signature of sanctity rather than an eccentric footnote to it.
christianity.tie_back: It gives the Christian form of the Kural's test: the mark of the genuinely holy is a gracious bearing toward every creature, not a status.
christianity.source: Bonaventure, Legenda Major XII.3 (the sermon to the birds); cf. the Canticle of the Creatures
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong on universal compassion as the badge of sanctity; described rather than quoted, and Christianity does not use it to redefine a priestly caste the way the Kural does.

islam.quote_or_event: “So, he went down the well again and filled his shoe with water and watered it. Allah thanked him for that deed and forgave him. The people said, ‘O Allah's Messenger! Is there a reward for us in serving the animals?’ He replied: ‘Yes, there is a reward for serving any animate (living being).’”
islam.explanation: A man's sins are forgiven for the single act of climbing back into a well to bring water to a thirsty dog, and the Prophet generalises the principle to every creature with a moist liver.
islam.tie_back: The same moral test as the Kural: standing before God turns on gracious conduct toward every living thing, including the least regarded.
islam._accuracy_note: Excellent: an explicit ruling that compassion extends to all living beings and is decisive for a person's standing, matching 'ev-uyirkkum' closely.

judaism.quote_or_event: “A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast: but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs uses treatment of animals as the diagnostic for righteousness, a verse the rabbis took as a scriptural anchor for the principle of tza'ar ba'alei chayim, the prohibition on causing animals distress.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it identifies the truly virtuous person by an attentiveness that reaches past human beings to other living creatures.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good: the same diagnostic (compassion to animals reveals the righteous), though it names a trait of the righteous rather than redefining a priestly title.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada's closing chapter systematically strips the word brahmana of every inherited and ritual meaning and reassigns it on the basis of conduct alone.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural's operation performed on the same word: anthanar / brahmana belongs to whoever lives rightly, not to whoever was born right.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Outstanding: identical rhetorical move on the identical contested term, and the surrounding verses (e.g. 405, on renouncing violence toward all beings) supply the Kural's compassion clause as well.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the last book of the Metamorphoses, Ovid gives Pythagoras a long speech urging humanity to stop slaughtering animals for food, arguing that souls pass between all bodies and that the ox which has worked the fields should not be repaid with the knife.
greek_mythology.explanation: The speech makes kinship with all animate life the ground of a specific ethical discipline, and presents it as the teaching of a sage set apart from ordinary appetite.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the nearest Greek-mythological articulation of the Kural's standard — the truly holy are known by a compassion that covers every living thing.
greek_mythology.source: Ovid, Metamorphoses XV.60-478 (the speech of Pythagoras)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A real and substantial parallel, though it sits at the edge of mythology proper — Ovid is dramatising a historical philosopher's doctrine inside a mythological poem.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In On Abstinence from Animal Food, Porphyry argues against the Stoic position that justice applies only between rational beings, holding instead that animals perceive, suffer and reason after their fashion, and that the philosopher's justice must therefore extend to every ensouled creature.
philosophy.explanation: Porphyry makes the scope of a person's justice the measure of their philosophical attainment, so that abstaining from harm to animals is not sentimentality but the completion of the ascetic life.
philosophy.tie_back: Same conclusion as the Kural: the person who deserves the highest title is the one whose gracious conduct excludes no living thing.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong philosophical parallel tying ascetic attainment to universal compassion; paraphrased because the argument runs across many chapters rather than sitting in one quotable line.
